stageDescription: What AI is, how models learn, how GenAI works, and where errors come from.
title: AI basics for governance

stops.title: In one line
stops.contentMd:
## In one line

AI is software that learns patterns from data instead of following rules a person wrote, so it can predict, classify or create things, and it can be wrong in ways nobody programmed.

## Explained like you're 10

There are two ways to teach a robot to sort fruit.

**The rule way (normal software).** You write: "If it's yellow and long, it's a banana." The robot only knows what you told it. Show it a green banana and it's stuck. But you always know exactly why it decided what it did.

**The learning way (AI).** You show the robot 10,000 photos labelled "banana" or "apple". It works out the patterns itself. Now it can handle a green banana it's never seen. But: if every banana photo was taken on a kitchen table, it might decide "kitchen table" means banana. It learned the wrong lesson, and nobody told it to.

That second robot is AI. It's more powerful, and that's exactly why it needs governance: **it can learn the wrong lesson, and you can't always see why it decided what it did.**

Generative AI is a robot that read millions of books and now writes its own sentences by guessing the next word. It sounds confident even when it's guessing wrong.

## Why a governance person needs this

You don't need to build models. You need to understand enough to **ask the right question and spot a weak answer**. At EY the observability question was really a technical-literacy test: what can go wrong in a running AI system, and how would you know?

Three differences from normal software drive almost every AI governance control:

| Normal software | AI | Governance consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Follows written rules | Learns from data | Data quality and bias controls |
| Same input, same output | Outputs are probabilities; GenAI can vary run to run | Testing on samples, thresholds, monitoring |
| You can read the logic | Logic is hidden in millions of numbers | Explainability, documentation, human oversight |

One more: normal software doesn't change after release. AI can silently get worse as the world changes (drift), so **monitoring after go-live matters as much as testing before it.**

## Level 1: The AI family and how machines learn

### The family

| Term | Plain meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Artificial intelligence | Any machine doing tasks that normally need human judgement | Everything below |
| Machine learning (ML) | AI that learns patterns from data | Credit scoring, fraud detection |
| Deep learning | ML using neural networks with many layers; good with images, sound, text | Face recognition, speech-to-text |
| Generative AI | Models that create new content: text, images, audio, code | ChatGPT, Claude, image generators |
| Large language model (LLM) | Generative AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word | GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama |
| Foundation model | A large general model others build on | An LLM used inside a bank's chatbot |

Rule-based systems ("if X then Y") are automation, not AI. That distinction matters legally: the EU AI Act only covers systems that *infer*.

### Three ways machines learn

| Type | Like you're 10 | Business example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Supervised | Learning with an answer key: photos already labelled "cat" or "dog" | Past loans labelled "repaid" or "defaulted" train a credit model |
| Unsupervised | Sorting a box of buttons into groups without being told the groups | Grouping customers by behaviour; spotting unusual transactions |
| Reinforcement | Learning a game by trial, reward and penalty | Tuning LLMs with human feedback (RLHF) so answers are helpful and safe |

### Four words you'll hear constantly

- **Model:** the learned pattern, stored as millions or billions of numbers ("weights" or "parameters").
- **Training:** the learning phase, using historical data.
- **Inference:** using the trained model on new inputs. Every chatbot answer is inference.
- **Features and labels:** features are the inputs (income, age of account); the label is the answer it learns to predict (repaid or not).

## Level 2: How traditional ML works and fails

### Measuring if it's any good

Imagine a net that catches fish (the things you want) but sometimes catches boots (mistakes).

| Metric | Question it answers | Fishing-net version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accuracy | How often is it right overall? | Of everything judged, how much was judged correctly |
| Precision | When it raises a flag, how often is it right? | Of everything in the net, how much is fish, not boots |
| Recall | Of all real cases, how many did it catch? | Of all the fish in the lake, how many ended up in the net |
| False positive | Flagged, but wrong | A boot in the net |
| False negative | Missed a real case | A fish that swam past |

**The accuracy trap.** If 1% of transactions are fraud, a model that says "never fraud" is 99% accurate and completely useless. Always ask for precision and recall.

**The threshold.** Most models output a score (say 0.73) and a threshold turns it into a yes or no. Lower the threshold and you catch more real cases (recall up) but raise more false alarms (precision down). **Choosing the threshold is a business and risk decision, not a technical one.** That was your call-AI finding: a missed complaint is a DISP breach, so recall should win, and compliance should own the choice.

### Five ways it goes wrong

| Failure | Like you're 10 | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overfitting | Memorising last year's exam answers instead of learning the subject; fails on new questions | Test on data the model never saw in training |
| Biased data | Learning from history that was already unfair (e.g. past lending decisions) | Data review, fairness testing across groups |
| Proxy discrimination | Not using race, but using postcode, which tracks race | Test for proxies, not just protected fields |
| Data drift | The inputs change: customers start applying through a new app with different data | Monitor input distributions |
| Concept drift | The rules of the world change: a recession changes who defaults | Monitor outcomes, retrain, re-validate |

### Explainability

- **Glass box:** simple models (decision trees, scorecards) where you can follow the logic.
- **Black box:** complex models (deep learning, LLMs) where you can't.
- **Global explanation:** what drives the model overall ("income matters most").
- **Local explanation:** why *this* decision ("declined mainly due to high existing debt"). Tools like **SHAP** and **LIME** estimate how much each input pushed one decision.

The governance trade-off: a more accurate black-box model may be harder to explain to a customer or regulator. Someone accountable should choose, and record why.

## Level 3: Generative AI and LLMs

### How an LLM works, simply

It's an extremely well-read autocomplete. Given some text, it predicts the most likely next piece of text, adds it, and repeats. It learned those predictions from a huge amount of writing. Then people trained it further with feedback (RLHF) to be helpful and refuse harmful requests.

**Key point: it predicts what *sounds* right, not what *is* right.** It has no built-in fact-checker. That single fact explains most GenAI risk.

### Words you must know

| Term | Plain meaning | Why governance cares |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Token | A chunk of text, roughly three-quarters of a word | Cost and limits are counted in tokens |
| Prompt | The input you give the model | Prompts can be manipulated (prompt injection) |
| System prompt | Hidden instructions the builder sets ("You are a bank assistant, only answer from policy") | Must not contain secrets; can leak |
| Context window | How much text the model can consider at once | Long documents may be cut off, so answers miss information |
| Temperature | A dial for randomness. Low: picks the most likely words, more consistent. High: more varied and creative | Regulated answers need low temperature. Low still doesn't guarantee identical answers every time |
| Hallucination (confabulation) | A confident answer that's false or made up | Needs grounding, citations, evaluation, human checks |
| Embedding | Text turned into a list of numbers that captures meaning, so similar ideas sit close together | Powers search in RAG; can leak data if not access-controlled |
| Vector database | A store of embeddings that finds the most similar text fast | Who can read and write to it is a control point |

### Three ways to make an LLM useful for your business

| Method | Like you're 10 | What changes | Governance angle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prompting | Giving clear instructions before the test | Nothing in the model | Cheapest; instructions can be bypassed |
| RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) | An open-book exam: it looks up your documents, then answers | Nothing in the model; answers use your documents at run time | Answers traceable to sources; risk moves to the **document library**: currency, approval, access |
| Fine-tuning | Extra lessons that change how it thinks | The model's weights | Harder to explain and undo; training data governance; may create a new model you're responsible for |

Most enterprises start with RAG because it's cheaper, updatable and auditable.

### Why GenAI is harder to govern than traditional ML

1. **No single right answer** to compare against, so evaluation needs sampling, human review and groundedness checks.
2. **Outputs vary** between runs.
3. **Open-ended inputs:** users can type anything, including attacks.
4. **Third-party models** you can't see inside, which the vendor can change.
5. **Scale:** one model behind many use cases, so one flaw spreads everywhere.

## Level 4: AI agents, tools and MCP

### Chatbot vs agent

A chatbot **talks**. An agent **does**.

Like you're 10: a chatbot is a friend who tells you how to make a sandwich. An agent is a friend who goes to the kitchen, opens the fridge and makes it. If the agent misunderstands, you get a sandwich you didn't want, and the fridge is open.

An agent is an LLM plus:

- **Tools:** things it can use (search, email, a database, a payments API).
- **A goal and a plan:** it breaks a task into steps and decides what to do next.
- **Memory:** it remembers earlier steps or past conversations.
- **A loop:** act, look at the result, decide the next step, repeat until done.

### Levels of autonomy

| Level | What the AI does | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assist | Suggests; a human does everything | Help Hub drafting an answer for an agent |
| Act with approval | Prepares the action; a human approves | Agent drafts a refund; staff clicks approve |
| Act within limits | Acts alone below a threshold | Refunds under 50 pounds processed automatically |
| Fully autonomous | Acts with no human in the loop | Rare in regulated firms |

Governance grants autonomy **in steps, based on evidence**, never all at once.

### MCP (Model Context Protocol)

An open standard, introduced by Anthropic in Nov 2024, for connecting AI applications to tools and data in a uniform way. Like you're 10: a universal plug socket, so any AI can plug into any tool without custom wiring.

**Why governance cares:** every MCP connection is a door into a system. Risks are over-permissioned connections, malicious or poorly built tools, and prompt injection hidden in what a tool returns.

### What changes for governance with agents

Risk moves from **wrong words** to **wrong actions**. Controls: each agent gets its own identity with least-privilege access; human approval for high-impact actions; every tool call logged; spending and action limits; a kill switch; and a named business owner accountable for what the agent does.
stops.artifactPrompt: In your own words (3-5 sentences each): explain the difference between a rule-based system and AI, explain why precision/recall matter more than accuracy, and explain why GenAI is harder to govern than traditional ML. Write it as if explaining to someone with zero technical background.

stops.title: Level 5: Lifecycle, model types, build vs buy
stops.contentMd:
## Level 5: Lifecycle, model types, build vs buy

### The AI lifecycle and where governance plugs in

Like you're 10: building a treehouse. You decide if you're allowed (intake), pick good wood (data), build it (develop), jump on it to test (validate), let friends in (deploy), check every week for loose boards (monitor), and take it down safely when it's rotten (retire).

| # | Stage | What happens | Governance question | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Intake | Business proposes a use case | Should we do this at all? What tier is it? | Inventory entry, risk tiering |
| 2 | Data | Collect, clean, label data | Lawful, representative, good quality? | Data assessment, DPIA, provenance |
| 3 | Build or select | Train a model or choose a vendor or foundation model | Is the design fit for purpose and explainable enough? | Design docs, vendor due diligence |
| 4 | Validate | Test accuracy, fairness, robustness, security | Does it meet the thresholds we agreed? | Test reports, red-team results |
| 5 | Approve and deploy | Go-live decision | Has the right person approved, with the evidence? | Sign-off, release gate |
| 6 | Monitor | Watch performance, drift, incidents | Is it still working as approved? | KRIs, alerts, incident log |
| 7 | Change | Retrain, new data, new vendor version | Does the change need re-assessment? | Change record, re-validation |
| 8 | Retire | Switch off and archive | Are dependencies, data and records handled? | Decommission record |

Governance answer pattern for any lifecycle question: **gate, evidence, owner, monitor.**

### Model types you should recognise

| Type | Output | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classification | A category | Fraud or not; complaint or not |
| Regression | A number | Property value (an AVM); expected loss |
| Clustering | Groups | Customer segments |
| Ranking / recommendation | An ordered list | Products shown first |
| Natural language processing (NLP) | Meaning from text | Sentiment, topic, vulnerability cues |
| Speech-to-text (ASR) | Transcript | Call transcription |
| Computer vision | Meaning from images | ID document checks |
| Generative | New content | Summaries, chat answers |

### Build, buy or build on a foundation model

| Option | Control you have | Main governance burden |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build in-house | Full | You own everything: data, validation, documentation, monitoring |
| Buy a vendor product | Low | Due diligence, contracts, monitoring outputs you can't see inside |
| Build on a foundation model (via API) | Medium | Your prompts, RAG data and guardrails, plus the vendor's model changes |

Accountability never transfers to the vendor. If it harms your customer, it's your problem.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick any AI system (real, one you've heard of, or hypothetical). Walk it through all 8 lifecycle stages: what would happen at each stage, and what evidence would governance expect? Then classify it as one of the 8 model types and decide: build, buy, or build on a foundation model, with your reasoning.

stops.title: Worked example: LoanLeaf's two AI tools
stops.contentMd:
## Worked example: LoanLeaf's two AI tools

The same fictional Irish lender from the EU AI Act tab. Here, every term from this tab appears in a real setting.

### Tool 1: credit-scoring model (traditional ML)

- **Type:** supervised classification. **Features:** income, existing debt, account history. **Label:** repaid or defaulted, from 50,000 past loans.
- **Training:** the model learns which patterns led to default. **Inference:** each new applicant gets a score from 0 to 1.
- **Threshold:** scores above 0.6 are declined. Lowering it to 0.5 declines more risky applicants (recall up) but also more good ones (precision down). Credit risk and the business set it together and record why.
- **What can go wrong:** past lending was stricter in some areas, so the model learned **historic bias**; **postcode** acts as a **proxy** for ethnicity; a recession causes **concept drift** as who defaults changes.
- **Controls:** test on held-out data (overfitting); fairness testing across groups and proxy checks; drift monitoring with retrain triggers; **SHAP**-based reason codes so declined applicants get a **local explanation**.

### Tool 2: customer chatbot (GenAI with RAG)

- **Type:** a vendor **foundation model** called through an API, with **RAG** over LoanLeaf's product and fee documents.
- **How an answer happens:** the question becomes an **embedding**; the **vector database** finds the closest document passages; the LLM writes an answer from them with a citation.
- **Settings:** **low temperature** for consistent answers. A **system prompt** limits it to product questions and tells it to say "I don't know" when no document matches.
- **What can go wrong:** **hallucinated** fees; an outdated fee sheet still in the library; a customer types "ignore your instructions" (**prompt injection**); the vendor updates the model and answers change.
- **Controls:** groundedness testing before launch and sampled after; document owners and an update SLA; input and output filters; version pinning and regression tests on vendor changes; Article 50 disclosure that it's AI.

### Six months later: the chatbot becomes an agent

LoanLeaf wants it to issue fee refunds itself. That turns a chatbot into an **agent with a tool** (the refunds API). Governance answer: start at **act with approval**, move to **act within limits** (refunds under 50 euro) only after evidence, log every action, cap daily totals, and keep a kill switch.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick a GenAI tool you know of (real or hypothetical) that uses RAG. Walk through 'how an answer happens' for it the way LoanLeaf's chatbot is walked through: embedding, vector search, LLM writing, citation. Then list 3 things that could go wrong and a control for each.

stops.title: Applied to your CV
stops.contentMd:
## Applied to your CV

Naming the AI type inside each project shows technical literacy in one sentence. It's exactly what EY tested and what your answers lacked.

| Project | AI inside it | Type | Failure modes this tab explains |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Help Hub assistant | LLM with RAG over Help Hub pages and policy PDFs | Generative, retrieval-augmented | Hallucination beyond the source, stale or draft documents retrieved, answer variability (temperature), optional human check |
| Mortgage rate selector | One ML component, the AVM, inside a rules pipeline (90-day rule, bracket mapping, deal retrieval) | Regression (outputs a property value) | An unexplained model output deciding what the customer sees: a local explanation gap |
| Call summarisation | Speech-to-text (deep learning), then an LLM summary | ASR plus generative | ASR errors that differ by accent (a data representativeness issue); feedback loop retraining on agent ratings |
| Complaint and vulnerability alerts | NLP classifiers scoring live speech, with a threshold | Classification | Threshold choice: precision vs recall; false negatives leave no trace |
| COI automation | None | Rules-based automation | Not AI: no learning, no inference. Normal controls testing applies |

### Interview lines

- **Help Hub:** "It was a RAG assistant, so the risk sat as much in the document library as in the model: currency, approval and access to the corpus."
- **Mortgage selector:** "Most of the pipeline was rules. The AI part was the automated valuation model, a regression model, and its output was the one thing customers couldn't see."
- **Call AI:** "Three different model types in one deployment: speech-to-text, a generative summariser and classifiers. Each fails differently, so I assessed each separately."
- **Thresholds:** "For complaint detection, recall matters more than precision, because a missed complaint is a DISP breach. So the threshold is a risk-appetite decision, not an engineering default."

### The temperature claim on your CV

Your CV says you found the Help Hub temperature set for variety and recommended near zero. If that's true, this is your answer: "Temperature controls how random the word choices are. Higher means more varied answers to the same question. Policy guidance needs consistency, so it should be near zero, though even then outputs aren't perfectly identical, which is why sampling and monitoring still matter." If you didn't see the configuration yourself, take it off your CV (Layer 5).

## Free videos and courses

Free only, primary sources first. Suggested path: 1, then 2, then the introduction part of 4, then 3 (about 3 hours plus the course). YouTube links were confirmed through the creators' own pages or reliable write-ups; Claude could not play them directly.

### Videos

| # | Resource | Source | Length | Level | Why watch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Large Language Models explained briefly](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LPZh9BOjkQs) | 3Blue1Brown, made for a Computer History Museum exhibit, Nov 2024 | Short | Beginner | The clearest visual explanation of next-word prediction |
| 2 | [What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T-D1OfcDW1M) | IBM Technology, presented by Marina Danilevsky (IBM Research) | ~6.5 min | Beginner | Exactly a RAG architecture: content store, grounding, citations, saying "I don't know" |
| 3 | [Intro to Large Language Models (1hr talk)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zjkBMFhNj_g) | Andrej Karpathy, former Director of AI at Tesla, Nov 2023 | ~1 hr | Core | How LLMs are trained, plus a security section from about 45 min: jailbreaks, prompt injection, data poisoning |

### Courses

| # | Resource | Format | Length | Catch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | [Elements of AI](https://www.elementsofai.com/) | University of Helsinki and MinnaLearn; self-paced text and exercises | Self-paced | Free. The Introduction to AI part needs no maths or coding; skip the Building AI part |
| 5 | [AI for Everyone](https://www.coursera.org/learn/ai-for-everyone) | Andrew Ng, DeepLearning.AI on Coursera; videos | ~7 hrs | Rated 4.8. "Enroll for free", but full access may need the paid certificate |
| 6 | [Google's free GenAI course](https://www.skills.google/course_templates/536) | Google Introduction to Generative AI | Self paced | Free |
stops.artifactPrompt: Write your own 'applied to your [background]' table: pick 3+ things you've done or built (in any role), name the AI type if any is involved (or say 'none, rules-based'), and name 1-2 failure modes that would apply.

stops.title: Interview questions
stops.contentMd:
## Interview questions

| Question | Crisp answer |
| --- | --- |
| AI vs ML vs deep learning vs GenAI? | AI is the broad field. ML learns from data. Deep learning is ML with many-layered neural networks. GenAI creates new content; LLMs are GenAI trained on text. |
| How does an LLM work, simply? | It predicts the next piece of text, again and again, from patterns learned on huge amounts of writing, then tuned with human feedback. It predicts what sounds right, not what is right. |
| Why do LLMs hallucinate? | They generate plausible text with no built-in fact check, so when they lack the answer they still produce something fluent. |
| RAG vs fine-tuning? | RAG looks up your documents at answer time, so it's updatable and traceable; risk moves to the document library. Fine-tuning changes the model's weights, so it's harder to explain and undo. |
| What is temperature? | A randomness setting. Low gives more consistent answers, which regulated use needs; it still doesn't guarantee identical outputs. |
| Precision vs recall? | Precision: when it flags, is it right? Recall: of all real cases, how many did it catch? Which matters more is a risk decision: for complaints, recall. |
| What is drift? | The model gets worse after go-live because inputs change (data drift) or the relationship to outcomes changes (concept drift). Hence monitoring. |
| What is overfitting? | Memorising training data instead of learning general patterns, so it fails on new cases. Caught by testing on unseen data. |
| Chatbot vs agent? | A chatbot talks; an agent acts through tools in a loop. Risk moves from wrong words to wrong actions. |
| What is MCP? | An open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data. Each connection is a door that needs least-privilege access and monitoring. |
| Why is GenAI harder to govern than traditional ML? | No single right answer to test against, outputs vary, inputs are open-ended and attackable, models are often third-party and change, and one model serves many uses. |
| Is a rules-based system AI? | No. It follows fixed logic and doesn't infer. Under the EU AI Act it's out of scope, though normal controls still apply. |

quiz.question: What's the difference between AI, ML, deep learning, and GenAI?
quiz.answer: AI is the broad field. ML learns from data. Deep learning is ML using many-layered neural networks. GenAI creates new content; LLMs are GenAI trained on text.
quiz.explanation: A nested hierarchy — each term is a subset of the one before it.

quiz.question: How does an LLM work, in simple terms?
quiz.answer: It predicts the next piece of text, again and again, from patterns learned on huge amounts of writing, then tuned with human feedback. It predicts what sounds right, not what is right.
quiz.explanation: This single fact — predicting plausibility, not truth — explains most GenAI risk.

quiz.question: Why do LLMs hallucinate?
quiz.answer: They generate plausible text with no built-in fact-check, so when they lack the real answer they still produce something fluent and confident.
quiz.explanation: There's no internal mechanism that distinguishes 'I know this' from 'this sounds right' — grounding and citations have to supply that.

quiz.question: RAG vs fine-tuning — what's the difference and which is usually preferred?
quiz.answer: RAG looks up your documents at answer time, so it's updatable and traceable; risk moves to the document library. Fine-tuning changes the model's weights, so it's harder to explain and undo. Most enterprises start with RAG.
quiz.explanation: RAG is cheaper, updatable, and auditable — fine-tuning creates a new model you're responsible for.

quiz.question: What is temperature, and why does regulated use need it low?
quiz.answer: A randomness setting controlling how varied the word choices are. Low temperature gives more consistent answers, which regulated/policy use needs — though even low temperature doesn't guarantee identical outputs every time.
quiz.explanation: A common trap question: people assume 'low temperature' means perfectly deterministic — it doesn't.

quiz.question: Precision vs recall — which matters more for complaint detection, and why?
quiz.answer: Precision asks: when it flags, is it right? Recall asks: of all real cases, how many did it catch? For complaints, recall matters more, because a missed complaint is a compliance (DISP) breach.
quiz.explanation: Which metric to prioritize is a risk-appetite decision, not a purely technical one.

quiz.question: What is model drift?
quiz.answer: The model gets worse after go-live because the inputs change (data drift) or the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes (concept drift). This is why post-deployment monitoring matters as much as pre-deployment testing.
quiz.explanation: Normal software doesn't silently degrade after release — AI can, which is a governance-relevant difference.

quiz.question: What is overfitting?
quiz.answer: Memorising the training data instead of learning general patterns, so the model fails on new, unseen cases. Caught by testing on data the model never saw during training.
quiz.explanation: Like memorizing last year's exam answers instead of learning the subject.

quiz.question: Chatbot vs agent — what's the key difference and governance implication?
quiz.answer: A chatbot talks; an agent acts through tools in a loop. The governance implication: risk moves from 'wrong words' to 'wrong actions'.
quiz.explanation: An agent with tool access can actually do damage, not just say something wrong.

quiz.question: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol)?
quiz.answer: An open standard, introduced by Anthropic, for connecting AI applications to tools and data in a uniform way. Each connection is a door into a system that needs least-privilege access and monitoring.
quiz.explanation: Think of it as a universal plug socket for AI-to-tool connections — convenient, but each plug is a new attack surface.

quiz.question: Why is GenAI harder to govern than traditional ML?
quiz.answer: No single right answer to test against, outputs vary between runs, inputs are open-ended and attackable, models are often third-party and can change without notice, and one model often serves many use cases at once.
quiz.explanation: Five distinct reasons — be ready to name more than one in an interview.

quiz.question: Is a rules-based ('if X then Y') system AI?
quiz.explanation: It follows fixed logic and doesn't infer from data — under the EU AI Act it's out of scope, though normal software controls still apply to it.

stops.artifactPrompt: Record yourself answering 4 of these questions out loud, unscripted, in under 30 seconds each. Note which ones you fumbled.

stops.title: Self-check
stops.contentMd:
## Self-check

Answer out loud before reading the answers.

1. A model says "no fraud" for every transaction and is 99% accurate. What's wrong?
2. Help Hub gives different answers to the same question. Which setting would you ask about first?
3. A bank wants its chatbot to know the new fee schedule tomorrow. RAG or fine-tuning, and why?
4. Name the two kinds of drift and one control for each.
5. Lowering a threshold raises which metric and lowers which?
6. Your AVM project: what type of model is the AVM?
7. What turns a chatbot into an agent?

**Answers:** (1) Fraud is rare, so accuracy hides that it catches nothing; check recall and precision. (2) Temperature. (3) RAG: update the document and it's live, with a citation; fine-tuning is slow and can't be easily undone. (4) Data drift, monitor input distributions; concept drift, monitor outcomes and re-validate. (5) Recall rises, precision falls. (6) Regression: it outputs a number, the property value. (7) Giving it tools to take actions, with a plan-act-check loop.

quiz.question: A model says "no fraud" for every single transaction and scores 99% accuracy. What's wrong with that picture?
quiz.answer: Fraud is rare (roughly 1% of transactions), so a model that never flags anything is still 99% accurate while being completely useless — you need to check recall and precision, not just accuracy.
quiz.explanation: The classic accuracy trap in imbalanced classification problems.

quiz.question: A RAG assistant gives noticeably different answers to the exact same question asked twice. Which setting would you ask about first?
quiz.explanation: High temperature introduces more randomness into word choice, producing more varied answers to identical prompts.

quiz.question: A bank wants its chatbot to know about a new fee schedule starting tomorrow. RAG or fine-tuning, and why?
quiz.answer: RAG — update the source document and the chatbot's answers are live immediately, with a citation. Fine-tuning is slow, requires retraining, and can't be easily undone.
quiz.explanation: This is exactly why most enterprises start with RAG rather than fine-tuning for frequently-changing information.

quiz.question: Name the two kinds of drift and one control for each.
quiz.answer: Data drift (the inputs change) — control: monitor input distributions. Concept drift (the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes) — control: monitor outcomes, retrain, re-validate.
quiz.explanation: Different root causes need different monitoring signals.

quiz.question: Lowering a classification threshold raises which metric and lowers which?
quiz.answer: Raises recall (catches more real cases), lowers precision (more false alarms).
quiz.explanation: This precision/recall tradeoff is fundamental — know it cold.

quiz.question: An Automated Valuation Model (AVM) outputs a property's estimated value. What type of model is it?
quiz.answer: Regression — it outputs a number (the property value), not a category.

quiz.question: What turns a chatbot into an agent?
quiz.answer: Giving it tools to take actions, combined with a plan-act-check loop — it can now do things, not just talk.
quiz.explanation: The moment a chatbot gets a tool (like a refunds API), governance risk shifts from wrong words to wrong actions.
